newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures finished MATIF trading weaker, but suffered less than other debt markets after the publication of strong U.S. job creation figures, buffered by continuing hopes of further interest rate reduction in France.
A trader at a large French bank said the fact that a number of banks were expecting a high U.S. jobs creation figure anyway helped mitigate the impact slightly..
"A lot was priced in already, that explains why it wasn't too bad," he said.

PIBOR interest rate futures, which shook off a spell in the doldrums to advance strongly this week, gained more ground on rate cut optimism, with March PIBOR reaching another contract high of 96.80 before settling at 96.78, up one basis point.

The March 10-year future, which started the MATIF day higher on the heels of German and U.S. debt, reached as high as 129.0 before going into reverse, but to a lesser degree than other markets after the U.S. data.
The U.S. payrolls report showing 262,000 jobs were created in December triggered a bond sell-off on fear of greater rate rise risk.
"December's labour market report was poor for bonds in every repect," Andrew Milligan at General Accident said in a note.

"Despite confident comments from Fed Governors about the inflation outlook, a Fed Funds rise in March must be on the cards," he said. Hours worked in December "suggests Q4 GDP growth of 3-4 percent, back towards the surge seen in Q2".

President Bill Clinton told reporters ahead of meeting top corporate executives the jobs data showed further evidence of U.S. economic strength. A lack of normal inflation pressure had been noted in recent talks with Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan and Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin.

Despite the data, 27 out of 29 economists polled by Reuters after the jobs release said they expected short-term rates to be kept unchanged when the Federal Open Market Committee meets on February 4 and 5.

Shielding France is a persistent market belief that a cut in interest rates from the Bank of France is on the cards, perhaps as early as next week, when the central bank's monetary policy council meets for the first time since appointment of two new members who markets feel up the chances of further rate cuts.
Many economists remain sceptical about the chances of a cut next Thursday, however.
